subject: Neurology
vignette: A medical student reviews the role of the thalamus as the brain's principal sensory relay station. She learns that nearly all ascending sensory pathways form synapses in specific thalamic nuclei before projecting to the cortex, but she recalls that one special sensory modality reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay.
question: Which of the following best describes the role of the thalamus in sensory processing?

options.text: It is the major relay for all ascending sensory information except olfaction
It relays every sensory modality, including olfaction, before cortical processing
It relays only visual and auditory information to the cortex
It is purely a motor structure with no role in sensory relay
It relays only pain and temperature sensation

explanation_correct: The thalamus is the major relay for all ascending sensory information except olfaction. Olfaction is the classic exception: CN I projects to the olfactory cortex without a thalamic relay. All other modalities—somatosensation, vision, hearing, and taste—synapse in specific thalamic nuclei before reaching primary cortices.

explanation_incorrect.B: Olfaction is the exception and reaches cortex without a thalamic relay, unlike other senses.
explanation_incorrect.C: The thalamus relays far more than vision and hearing; it also handles somatosensory and gustatory information.
explanation_incorrect.D: The thalamus has a major sensory relay role, and VA/VL nuclei also participate in motor circuits.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pain and temperature are only part of the spinothalamic input; the thalamus relays many other modalities.

educationalObjective: The thalamus relays all ascending sensory information except olfaction, which bypasses a thalamic relay.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient sustains a small lesion in a thalamic nucleus and loses vibration sense, pain and temperature perception, pressure, light touch, and proprioception over the body, sparing the face. The damaged nucleus normally receives input from both the spinothalamic tract and the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway.
question: Which thalamic nucleus is most likely lesioned?

options.text: Ventral posteromedial nucleus
Lateral geniculate nucleus
Medial geniculate nucleus
Ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei
Ventral posterolateral nucleus; it relays spinothalamic and dorsal column input to the primary somatosensory cortex

explanation_correct: The ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus receives spinothalamic and dorsal column/medial lemniscus afferents and relays vibration, pain, pressure, proprioception, light touch, and temperature from the body to the primary somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe. A VPL lesion therefore causes body-wide (nonfacial) loss of these modalities.

explanation_incorrect.A: The ventral posteromedial nucleus handles face sensation and taste via trigeminal and gustatory pathways, not body sensation.
explanation_incorrect.B: The lateral geniculate nucleus relays visual information from CN II to the occipital cortex.
explanation_incorrect.C: The medial geniculate nucleus relays auditory information to the temporal cortex.
explanation_incorrect.D: The VA/VL nuclei relay basal ganglia and cerebellar motor output to frontal motor cortices, not somatosensation.

educationalObjective: The VPL nucleus relays body spinothalamic and dorsal column sensation (pain, temperature, vibration, proprioception) to primary somatosensory cortex.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient loses sensation over the face and the ability to taste after a small thalamic infarct. The affected nucleus normally receives trigeminal afferents for facial sensation and gustatory afferents for taste.
question: Which thalamic nucleus is most likely affected?

options.text: Ventral posterolateral nucleus
Ventral posteromedial nucleus; it relays trigeminal face sensation and taste
Lateral geniculate nucleus
Medial geniculate nucleus
Ventral lateral nucleus

explanation_correct: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus receives trigeminal and gustatory pathways and relays face sensation and taste to the primary somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe. The mnemonic 'very pretty makeup goes on the face' captures VPM's role in facial sensation, in contrast to VPL for the body.

explanation_incorrect.A: The VPL nucleus relays body sensation from the spinothalamic and dorsal column pathways, not facial sensation or taste.
explanation_incorrect.C: The lateral geniculate nucleus is the visual relay for CN II to the occipital cortex.
explanation_incorrect.D: The medial geniculate nucleus is the auditory relay to the temporal cortex.
explanation_incorrect.E: The ventral lateral nucleus relays cerebellar and basal ganglia motor output, not sensory face or taste information.

educationalObjective: The VPM nucleus relays trigeminal facial sensation and taste to primary somatosensory cortex.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A medical student reviews the specific thalamic nuclei and wants to match each one with its input pathway and cortical projection target. She is careful to distinguish the visual, auditory, and motor relays from one another.
question: Which of the following correctly matches a thalamic nucleus with its input and cortical destination?

options.text: Lateral geniculate nucleus receives auditory input from the inferior colliculus and projects to the auditory cortex
Medial geniculate nucleus receives visual input from CN II and projects to the visual cortex

Lateral geniculate nucleus relays CN II optic tract visual information to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe, while the medial geniculate nucleus relays hearing to the temporal lobe and VA/VL nuclei relay basal ganglia and cerebellar motor output to frontal cortices
Ventral posterolateral nucleus relays visual information to the occipital cortex
Ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei relay olfactory information to the frontal cortex

explanation_correct: The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) receives CN II, optic chiasm, and optic tract input and projects vision to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe ('lateral = light'). The medial geniculate nucleus relays hearing to the temporal cortex ('medial = music'), and the VA/VL nuclei relay basal ganglia and cerebellar motor output to frontal motor cortices.

explanation_incorrect.A: Auditory input from the inferior colliculus goes to the medial geniculate nucleus, not the lateral geniculate nucleus.
explanation_incorrect.B: Visual input from CN II goes to the lateral geniculate nucleus, not the medial geniculate nucleus.
explanation_incorrect.D: The VPL nucleus relays body somatosensation to the parietal somatosensory cortex, not vision to the occipital cortex.
explanation_incorrect.E: The VA/VL nuclei relay motor output from basal ganglia and cerebellum; olfaction has no thalamic relay.

educationalObjective: LGN relays vision to occipital cortex, MGN relays hearing to temporal cortex, and VA/VL relay motor output to frontal cortex.
